items.prompt: Describe the difference between HIV and AIDS.
items.canonical_answer: HIV is the virus that attacks the immune system. AIDS is not a separate virus but a syndrome: the most advanced stage of HIV infection. In AIDS the immune system is so weak that the body cannot fight opportunistic infections such as tuberculosis, whereas a person can live with HIV for many years without developing AIDS, especially on treatment.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for the relationship: HIV is the virus attacking the immune system.
1 mark for the pattern of progression: AIDS is the advanced stage/syndrome, not a virus.
1 mark for evidence of the difference: the immune system cannot fight opportunistic infections, or HIV need not mean AIDS.

items.prompt: Explain the error in calling AIDS a virus separate from HIV. What distinction tests the terms?

marking_guidance: 1 mark for the virus/syndrome error; 1 for the correct distinction and discriminating classification test.

items.prompt: Explain how poorly managed illness can affect a household’s resources where it interrupts earnings and adds care costs.
items.canonical_answer: Illness can reduce available working time and earnings while increasing relevant expenses. Less money remains for other needs under those conditions. Effective care, income support and fair access can change the pathway, so the outcome is not inherent to HIV status.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for illness/access conditions as a factor; 1 for the income/cost link; 1 for reduced available funds; 1 for the conditional household effect and relevant response.

items.prompt: How far do you agree that providing free antiretroviral treatment is the most important effort the Namibian government makes against HIV and AIDS?
items.canonical_answer: Agree to a large extent. Free ART in public facilities since 2003 keeps people living with HIV alive and able to work, cuts AIDS deaths among 15 to 49 year olds and means fewer children are orphaned. People taking ART who maintain an undetectable viral load do not transmit HIV sexually, so treatment also prevents new infections. However, ART alone does not stop people becoming infected: free condoms, testing, prevention of mother-to-child transmission and awareness campaigns are needed to reduce new cases, and treatment is a large lifelong cost. Overall ART is the most important single effort for saving lives, but it works best combined with prevention.
marking_guidance: Up to 2 C marks for evidence supporting ART (survival, workforce, fewer orphans, treatment as prevention).
Up to 2 C marks for evidence that other efforts matter (prevention to stop new infections, cost, testing).
1 C mark for a reasoned overall judgement.

items.prompt: How far do you agree that the Namibian government should spend more on preventing HIV than on treating it?
items.canonical_answer: Partly agree. Prevention through free condoms, testing, prevention of mother-to-child transmission and education for young people reduces new infections, so fewer people need lifelong treatment later, and preventing infections can reduce future treatment costs, although the cost-effectiveness of each programme must be assessed. However, treatment keeps many people alive and working, protects children from becoming orphans, and itself prevents sexual transmission when treatment maintains an undetectable viral load, so cutting it would raise deaths and new infections. Prevention deserves more attention, but both must be funded together.
marking_guidance: Up to 2 C marks for evidence for prevention (fewer new infections, lower long-term cost, named prevention efforts).
Up to 2 C marks for evidence for treatment (survival, workforce, orphans, treatment as prevention).
1 C mark for a reasoned overall judgement.

items.prompt: How far do you agree that NGOs do more than local authorities to help people affected by HIV and AIDS in Namibia?
items.canonical_answer: Partly agree. NGOs give direct help: counselling and testing, home-based care for the sick, food and emotional support for people on treatment, and support for orphans; their volunteers reach remote villages. However, many NGOs depend on donor funding that can stop. Local authorities provide permanent town services and land, include HIV in local planning and take part in the regional committees that coordinate the response. NGOs do more face-to-face care, while local authorities provide the lasting framework, so each helps in a different way.
marking_guidance: Up to 2 C marks for evidence of NGO contributions and their limits.
Up to 2 C marks for evidence of local-authority contributions and their limits.
1 C mark for a reasoned overall judgement.

items.prompt: How far do you agree that churches play an important part in reducing the impact of HIV and AIDS in Namibia?
items.canonical_answer: Agree to a large extent. Churches have large congregations across Namibia, so they reach many people. They provide counselling, home visits and care for the sick, help orphans with food and school costs, and can reduce stigma and encourage testing; some faith-based institutions also provide treatment. However, churches cannot replace medical services, and some religious messages discourage condom use or present HIV as a moral failing, which can increase stigma. Their role is important mainly in care and support, alongside health services.
marking_guidance: Up to 3 C marks for evidence of ways churches help (reach, care, orphans, stigma, testing, treatment).
Up to 1 C mark for a limitation supported by a reason (not medical care; some messages increase stigma or discourage condoms).
1 C mark for a reasoned overall judgement.

items.prompt: Explain how wider use of antiretroviral drugs can change Namibia's population structure.
items.canonical_answer: ARVs suppress HIV, so fewer people develop AIDS and the death rate falls. Fewer adults aged 15 to 49 die, so the working-age bars of the pyramid stay wide and fewer children are orphaned. Life expectancy rises, so more people reach old age and the top of the pyramid widens. With fewer deaths and births continuing, population growth can increase slightly.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for the factor: ARVs reduce deaths/the death rate.
1 mark for the link: fewer adult deaths, because working-age bars stay wide or fewer children are orphaned.
1 mark for the effect of higher life expectancy: a wider top of the pyramid.
1 mark for the result of faster population growth.

items.prompt: Describe how increased condom use can change the shape of Namibia's population pyramid.
items.canonical_answer: Fewer unplanned pregnancies lower the birth rate, so the base of the pyramid becomes narrower. Fewer HIV infections mean fewer young adults die, so the working-age bars stay wide. Over time more people survive into the older age groups, so the upper bars can become wider. The net effect on growth depends on the birth and death changes.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for the pattern of a narrower base, with evidence of a lower birth rate.
1 mark for wider working-age bars because of fewer AIDS deaths.
1 mark for the trend towards more people in older age groups (do not require a fixed net growth effect).

items.prompt:
A hypothetical eligible group contains 100 people living with HIV. Eighty know their status and sixty-four receive treatment. Fifty-eight of those sixty-four have the stated suppression outcome. No outcome for untreated people is supplied.
(a) Name the treatment category used to suppress HIV. [1]
(b) Calculate treatment coverage among the eighty diagnosed people. [2]
(c) Describe three distinct features of the cascade using the correct denominators. [3]
(d) What judgement is supported about the claim “eighty per cent of all 100 are receiving treatment”? [1]
items.canonical_answer: (a) Antiretroviral therapy. (b) 64/80 = 0.8, equivalent to 80%. (c) Eighty of 100 know their status; sixty-four of 100 receive treatment; fifty-eight of sixty-four treated have the stated suppression outcome, about 90.6% of that subgroup. (d) Reject the claim: treatment among all 100 is 64%, while 80% uses the diagnosed subgroup denominator.
marking_guidance: (a) 1 A mark for ART.
(b) 2 B marks for the diagnosed-group method and correct percentage.
(c) 3 B marks for three distinct cascade patterns with appropriate resource evidence and denominators.
(d) 1 C mark for the supported denominator judgement.

items.prompt: In 2017 adult HIV prevalence (ages 15 to 64) was 22.3% in Zambezi, 17.9% in Ohangwena, 8.3% in Khomas and 7.6% in Kunene; the national figure was 12.6%. How far do you agree that Zambezi had the highest prevalence of these regions mainly because of its transport routes and borders? [5]
items.canonical_answer: Transport and borders are a plausible part of the explanation: Zambezi borders Zambia and Botswana, and the Trans-Caprivi Highway crosses it through Katima Mulilo. The figures cannot show that they are the main cause. Mobility can separate partners, connect sexual networks and interrupt prevention or treatment; unprotected sex can then transmit HIV. However, travel and ordinary social contact do not themselves transmit it. The regional percentages measure prevalence, reflecting past infection as well as age, sex, migration and survival on treatment. Zambezi also has a wide estimate interval (17.5–27.0%). Evidence on exposure and service access is needed before ranking causes. Therefore the transport explanation deserves investigation, but its primacy is unproven.
marking_guidance: Up to 2 C marks for explaining a plausible mobility-related exposure or service-access mechanism linked to Zambezi's borders or route.
Up to 2 C marks for explaining limits of regional prevalence as causal evidence, alternative influences or sampling uncertainty.
1 C mark for a supported judgement; do not require agreement that transport is the main cause.
